articles.title: From transcript to tasks: how automatic action-item extraction actually works
articles.excerpt: I'm the maker of MeetNote — an AI meeting-notes app (free on Google Play) that records calls, transcribes them, and turns them into decisions and action items. Here's what I learned building the extra…
articles.body: I'm the maker of MeetNote — an AI meeting-notes app (free on Google Play) that records calls, transcribes them, and turns them into decisions and action items. Here's what I learned building the extraction side of it. Every meeting ends the same way: someone says "I'll send that over," someone else nods, and by Monday nobody remembers who promised what. The transcript has the answer — but a 45-minute transcript is not a to-do list. This is how we think about turning raw meeting text into decisions and action items that people actually follow up on. 1. The transcript is the easy part Speech-to-text is a solved-ish problem. Modern models handle multiple speakers, accents, and background noise well enough that the transcript is rarely the bottleneck.

articles.body: Have you ever pushed code to a repository, only to have your CI/CD pipeline fail because of a SonarQube Quality Gate ? Understanding how SonarQube evaluates code does not just help pass automated checks—it makes it easier to catch reliability, security, and maintainability issues before an analysis even runs. This guide breaks down SonarQube’s core architecture, how it calculates A–E ratings , what Technical Debt actually represents, and how to spot common flaws across JavaScript, React, and SQL . 1. The 4 Issue Categories: What Question to Ask? SonarQube classifies code issues into four main categories. Each category answers a specific question about the code: Category Core Question Example Bug Could this cause the program to behave incorrectly or crash?

articles.title: A solver froze our Node server for 8 seconds in CI — moving it off the request path
articles.excerpt: I build VSolitaire, a free solitaire site. Its Daily challenge gives every player the same Klondike deal each day (Draw 3, with a new deal at 00:00 UTC). Until this month that deal was a random shuffl…
articles.body: I build VSolitaire, a free solitaire site. Its Daily challenge gives every player the same Klondike deal each day (Draw 3, with a new deal at 00:00 UTC). Until this month that deal was a random shuffle nobody had checked, and on some days nobody won it. So I made the server pick a deal that a solver can win. It passed the unit tests and CI on its own branch. Then it froze the whole API in an end-to-end test. Here is how I found the problem and what I changed. The change The Daily's seed comes from the date. The new version tries up to 20 candidate seeds for a date and keeps the first one my Klondike solver wins at Draw 3. If none of the 20 wins, it falls back to the first. The search is capped by nodes, never by time.

articles.title: Name the Owner Before You Build
articles.excerpt: Originally published at Trida AI. The first deliverable of a deployment is not a prototype. It is three names, written down, with the decisions each of those people is allowed to make. Most kickoffs p…
articles.body: Originally published at Trida AI . The first deliverable of a deployment is not a prototype. It is three names, written down, with the decisions each of those people is allowed to make. Most kickoffs produce the other artefacts easily enough: a sponsor, a budget, a target date, a slide with the workflow drawn on it. A sponsor can approve spend and unblock a room. What a sponsor usually cannot do is answer the questions that start arriving once the system is live and changing. Who may widen what the system is allowed to touch? Who decides that a cheaper model is good enough for this step, and who carries it when the cheaper model is wrong? Who can pause the thing on a bad Tuesday? Those questions arrive whether or not anyone was named to answer them.

articles.title: What's next for NASA interstellar Voyager 1 probe after passing 1 light-day from Earth?
articles.excerpt: The Voyager 1 probe continues to fly out into interstellar space after its historic distance milestone. NASA expects it to keep working until at least 2027.
articles.body: Voyager 1 has reached a historic milestone in space — it now takes a light-day to send a command to the spacecraft, meaning a full 24 hours for Earth to hail the distant spacecraft. Since Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2 , launched on an initial tour through the outer solar system in 1977, their missions have been packed with science. Voyager 1 looked at Jupiter and Saturn from up close before veering for a flyby of Saturn's moon Titan and Saturn's rings, a pathway that brought it above the plane of the solar system in the early 1980s. Voyager 1's faster path out of the solar system brought it to one light-day in distance on Wednesday (Nov. 18), while Voyager 2 — which took a slightly slower track to see Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — will reach a light-day of distance in 2035.

articles.body: Elon Musk said Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy is lying about disruptions to Starshield in Ukraine and that he's trying to misuse SpaceX's consumer service, Starlink, for military purposes. Musk made the comments at The New York Times ' DealBook Summit on Wednesday as he tried to explain the conflict following weeks of back and forth between Zelenskyy, Musk, and the US government. articles.title: NASA Sets Coverage for Northrop Grumman CRS-25 Launch, Prelaunch
articles.excerpt: NASA, Northrop Grumman, and SpaceX are targeting no earlier than 10:47 a.m. EST, Sunday, Nov. 29, for the next launch delivering science investigations, supplies, and equipment to the International Sp…
articles.body: NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 24 mission launched Saturday, April 11, 2026, aboard the company’s Cygnus XL spacecraft atop a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission will deliver approximately 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International Space Station. Credit: Northrop Grumman NASA, Northrop Grumman, and SpaceX are targeting no earlier than 10:47 a.m. EST, Sunday, Nov. 29, for the next launch delivering science investigations, supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station. The agency also will hold a prelaunch media teleconference on Monday, Nov. 23.
